title: bench-harness-checkerboard-priming-notes
content:
Purpose
This is a working note for a new warmup/priming methodology we want to trial across multi-GPU fixtures: the 'checkerboard priming' pattern. The goal: produce repeatable steady-state throughput with minimized thermal/jitter fallout, and a clear signal-to-noise ratio for unit comparisons (quantization, kernel selection, batch shapes).

Why different from existing warmup recipes
- Most playbooks we have use monotonic ramps, staircase priming, or seed-anchored replay sequences. Those are good but we still see run-to-run throughput variance tied to ordering of sequence lengths and microburst alignment.
- Checkerboard priming intentionally interleaves high-occupancy and low-occupancy requests in a regular pattern to exercise routing, batch coalescing, KV cache behavior and thermal settling in parallel. The hypothesis: a structured alternation reduces stateful path bias (e.g., hot CUDA kernels staying resident) and surfaces caching edge cases earlier.

High-level pattern
- Pattern element: [long-context, short-context, long-context, short-context, ...] where long_context ≈ 2x median sequence length for workload and short_context ≈ 0.25x median.
- Packets of N elements form a 'checkerboard block' (~64 requests) that gets replayed during warmup. Between blocks add short randomized jitter (0–3 ms) to emulate real client jitter and avoid lockstep artifacts from perfectly periodic injection.

Experiment matrix (example configs)
- Fixture types: A100-80GB x1, A100-80GB x4, H100 x1, H100 x8 (mix of 16GB/80GB reserved nodes).
- Model variants: fp16 baseline, int8 quantized, mqa-compat variant.
- Block sizes to test: 32, 64, 128.
- Checkerboard ratios: 1:1, 2:1 (two longs per short), 3:1.
- Warmup repetitions: 1 block, 5 blocks, 20 blocks.
- Seed hygiene: PRNG seed rotated per-run vs seed-fixed.

Metrics to capture (required)
- token/s (sliding 15s windows), p50/p90/p99 latency per-token and per-request, GPU utilization (SM%, memory BW), GPU power, host-side CPU % and IO wait, kernel occupancy (if available from CUPTI/NVIDIA tools), batch formation latency, KV cache hit/miss ratio (if instrumented).
- Derived signals: steady-state window start time (time when token/s variance drops below 3%), plateau drift (percent change over 10m), thermal-induced throttles, and failed inference count (timeout/retry).

Run procedure (play-by-play)
1) Fixture boot and health checks. Confirm driver + CUDA + cuDNN versions match bench baseline.
2) Clear caches: restart serving instances to avoid prior-run contamination. Note: aim to test both cold start and restarted-with-cache scenarios in separate experiments.
3) Start tracing hooks (traces to file, and metrics to Prometheus endpoint).
4) Deploy checkerboard block to loadgen with configured jitter. Start with block size 64, ratio 1:1, 5 repetitions.
5) Observe sliding throughput until plateau. Mark plateau start. Keep running for an observation window (recommended 10m).
6) After run, collect traces, host and GPU telemetry, loadgen logs (with timestamps aligned to NTP).

Repeatability hygiene
- Clock sync: all hosts MUST be NTP-synced within 50ms; ideally use chrony and capture offset. Include timestamp correction metadata with every run.
- RNG hygiene: two modes: deterministic seed (for exact replay) and seed-rotated (for statistical coverage). Document which mode used in the run name.
- Client emulator variance: vary inter-arrival jitter seed families across >5 runs to estimate sampling variance. Don't rely on a single run.

Warmup length heuristics and failure cases
- Heuristic: run until 3 consecutive 15s sliding windows have mean throughput within 2% and latency p90 within 5% of preceding window. Cap warmup to 20 minutes.
- Failure modes: long ramp despite stability heuristics (likely thermal or GC-related), oscillation between two throughput modes (indicates scheduler thrashing or batching instability), sudden drop-offs after long run (thermal throttling or memory fragmentation).
- Quick mitigations: reduce block size to avoid hitting batch coalescing limits; insert short cool-down pause (30s) to allow thermal recovery and re-prime; toggle kernel selection (fallback to older kernel) if available.

Analysis checklist (post-run)
- Correlate batch size histogram with token/s spikes. Is batch coalescing consistent with expected occupancy?
- Inspect kernel timelines: are heavy kernels repeated in long-phase only? Checkerboard should distribute kernel load.
- Compare seed-fixed runs: are traces nearly identical in microsecond-level ordering? If not, investigate sources of non-determinism (epoll ordering, thread scheduling).
- Thermal vs algorithmic regressions: if slowdown correlates with GPU power/thermal rise, mark as thermal; otherwise dig into runtime scheduling and cache thrash.

Dashboard/KPIs to add to the bench harness UI
- 'Checkerboard index' = variance reduction metric comparing checkerboard warmup vs monotonic ramp (lower is better).
- 'Plateau time' (time to steady-state), 'Plateau stability' (% variance in plateau window), and 'Reproducibility score' (cross-run correlation of per-request latency quantiles).

Open questions / TODOs
- Is checkerboard priming useful for models with heavy KV-cache reuse (long sessions)? Should we adapt ratio based on expected real-world session lengths? (P0: run with chat-like long-session traces.)
- Need a script to convert real production traces into checkerboard-friendly blocks (privacy-preserving sampling).
- Evaluate whether introducing small memory pressure during warmup (background preemptible tasks) surfaces fragmentation issues earlier.

Run naming convention (proposed)
- bench.checkerboard.<fixture>.<model>.<blockSz>.<ratio>.<reps>.<seedMode>.<YYYYMMDDHHMM>
  e.g. bench.checkerboard.a100x4.fp16.64.1to1.5.seedfixed.20241003T0930

Notes to self (scratchpad)
- Marco to instrument batch formation latency in client emulator (ticket ENG-1198).
- Dana to capture CUPTI kernel timelines and map to model op names.
- Add a flag in loadgen to insert 0-3ms jitter between requests inside block.

References and inspiration
- Prior staircase priming notes (see runbook directory) but this intentionally swaps monotonic ramp for structured alternation.
- Internal thermal tuning experiments (July 2024) showed oscillation reduced when interleaving memory-heavy and compute-heavy requests; checkerboard tries to generalize that insight.

Summary
This doc is a live working note. The checkerboard priming pattern is experimental but promising for improving repeatability across fixtures by preventing state bias during warmup. Next step: schedule a matrix run (small) on a100x1 and a100x4 next week, collect 10 runs each, and compare against staircase baseline.

Unresolved: best ratio for chat-biased workloads and how to integrate with KV-prefetching optimizations.
